content: Subjects with occult hepatitis B infection can serve as a potential source of new infections in blood transfusion services if hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is used as the sole marker for screening donor populations. Reactivation of hepatitis B virus (HBV) can occur spontaneously or be triggered by cancer chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive therapies, potentially leading to fatal acute-on-chronic hepatitis. To prevent this, preemptive therapy with nucleos(t)ide analogues is often employed. Approximately 20% of individuals with hepatitis B develop significant extrahepatic manifestations, which can impact their quality of life and mortality. These manifestations and their management have been reviewed extensively. Treatment with nucleoside analogues has improved outcomes for HBsAg-positive individuals with glomerulonephritis, kidney transplant recipients, and those on dialysis, enhancing survival without negatively affecting renal graft outcomes. Arthritis associated with HBV infection has been reported to resolve following a reduction in HBV replication. Since 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that all infants receive 3–4 doses of the HBV vaccine, with the first dose administered within 24 hours of birth. Most WHO member states include the HBV vaccine in their Expanded Programme on Immunization. Preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) from highly viremic mothers requires not only birth-dose vaccination but also preemptive antiviral therapy for the mother. In countries with intermediate or low HBV endemicity, a significant disease burden arises from acute and chronic infections acquired during childhood, adolescence, or adulthood. Target groups for catch-up vaccination and other preventive strategies include young adolescents, household and sexual contacts of HBsAg-positive individuals, and those at risk of acquiring HBV infection. WHO and other international guidelines recommend screening high-risk groups for HBsAg and offering hepatitis B vaccination to those at risk who are not immune. High-risk groups include household and sexual contacts of individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), people living with HIV, individuals who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, indigenous populations, incarcerated individuals, and transgender people. Blood and organ donors should also be screened for HBsAg and other bloodborne pathogens to prevent HBV transmission, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Population-based screening is recommended for migrants from endemic regions. Routine HBsAg screening of all pregnant women is advised as part of integrated antenatal care services, including screening for syphilis and HIV. Testing approaches should leverage existing facility-based or community-based opportunities. HBV DNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) is recommended following a reactive HBsAg test to guide treatment decisions and monitor treatment response. Dried blood spot specimens may be considered for testing in certain settings. HBsAg-positive individuals should undergo routine assessment to guide management and determine the need for treatment. This includes evaluating additional serological markers (e.g., HBeAg), measuring aminotransferase levels to assess liver inflammation, quantifying HBV DNA levels, and determining liver fibrosis stage using non-invasive tests such as the AST-to-platelet ratio index (APRI), transient elastography (FibroScan®), or FibroTest. Clinical evaluation for cirrhosis and decompensation, along with laboratory tests (e.g., bilirubin, albumin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, prothrombin time, and platelet count), is essential. HBV activity can vary over time, but the degree of hepatic fibrosis determines prognosis. Non-invasive methods for assessing liver disease stage have largely replaced liver biopsy. Quantifying HBsAg levels has been proposed to determine prognosis and monitor treatment response. Viral DNA detection remains the optimal method for quantifying HBV viremia and monitoring replication during antiviral therapy. Treatment with nucleoside analogues has been shown to delay cirrhosis progression, reduce HCC incidence, and improve long-term survival. Long-term, potentially lifelong, nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy is required in most cases. Antiviral drugs such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir (ETV), and tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) are highly potent against HBV and have a high barrier to resistance. Research is ongoing to develop curative therapies for HBV that eliminate all replicative forms, including covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), and reduce the need for lifelong treatment. People with hepatitis B often face barriers to accessing care and treatment, including limited availability of diagnostics, specialist care models, and out-of-pocket expenses. Stigma and discrimination associated with hepatitis B can lead to social exclusion, relationship instability, and difficulties in employment or education. Provider training is essential to reduce stigma, improve communication, and emphasize the importance of disease management and monitoring. The WHO guidelines on hepatitis B testing, care, and treatment were developed using the GRADE approach, which evaluates the quality of evidence and formulates recommendations. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of benefits and harms, resource requirements, and other factors. High-quality evidence supports strong recommendations, while conditional recommendations may reflect uncertainty or smaller benefits relative to harms.
